pages.p: New devices bootstrap from a prebuilt, CDN-served snapshot per scope, then pull deltas from its cursor. Partial replication keeps each device to the data its user needs, and imports stream, batch and defer indexing. First sync goes from hours of paging to minutes.

title: Android in depth
blurb: WorkManager, long transfers and the limits OEMs add.

pages.p: WorkManager stores your work in its own database, survives process death and reboots, applies constraints and retries with backoff. It chooses the right system scheduler for each Android version. It is the default answer for deferrable background work.

Enqueue sync under a **unique name** with a KEEP or APPEND policy, so ten triggers in a minute become one job, not ten. Give each file upload its own unique name, such as upload- followed by the file ID.

Declare what the job needs: a network, an unmetered network for media, battery not low. Periodic work runs at most every 15 minutes and may wait in Doze. For sync right after a user action, use expedited work that falls back to normal work when its quota runs out.

A worker reads its progress from the database, does a bounded amount of work, commits after each unit and checks isStopped. If the system stops it, it returns retry and the next run continues exactly where it left off.
pages.ex: Never do network work inside the FCM callback. Enqueue a worker instead.

pages.p: On Android, sync runs in WorkManager under unique names, with network and battery constraints and exponential backoff. Workers are short, checkpoint after every unit and return retry when stopped. FCM messages only enqueue work; they never make the network call themselves.

Android 12 stopped most apps from starting foreground services in the background. Android 14 requires each one to declare a type, such as dataSync. Android 15 limits dataSync services to about six hours in every 24. A long-running service is no longer a safe default.

From Android 14, a job started while the user is in your app can be marked **user-initiated**. It shows a notification, may run for a long time and is not bound by normal job quotas. It exists for exactly the big upload or download a user asked for.
The required notification should be useful: file name, percentage and a cancel button. If the user cancels, record it in your database so the transfer is not quietly restarted later.

For big transfers the user starts, we use user-initiated data transfer jobs on Android 14 and later, with a progress notification and a cancel action. We avoid depending on dataSync foreground services because of the type requirement and Android 15’s six-hour daily limit.

reels.title: Doze, standby buckets and OEM killers

pages.p: When the phone sits still with its screen off, Doze batches background work into short maintenance windows. Jobs and alarms wait, so your sync may run minutes or hours later than you expected.
Android ranks apps by recent use: active, working set, frequent, rare and restricted. Apps in the rare bucket get very few job runs and a limited number of high-priority FCM messages.

Some manufacturers add their own aggressive killers. Test on Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo and Samsung phones, measure background runs per manufacturer, and guide users of critical apps to allow background activity.
If the user taps Force Stop in settings, every scheduled job and alarm is cancelled until they open the app again. Nothing you write can undo that.
pages.ex: Test with adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle, and am set-standby-bucket to simulate rare.

pages.p: We plan for Doze, standby buckets and OEM battery managers rather than fighting them. Sync health is tracked per manufacturer, we test on Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo and Samsung, and users of critical features get a short guide to allow background activity.

title: iOS in depth
blurb: Background tasks, background URLSession and the traps.

pages.p: **BGAppRefreshTask** gives you about 30 seconds to fetch small updates. **BGProcessingTask** gives minutes for heavier work, usually overnight while charging. You request them; iOS decides when, based on battery, network and how the user uses your app.

Register handlers at launch. In each handler, schedule the next task first, then do bounded work. Set an expiration handler that cancels the work, and always call setTaskCompleted. Apps that overrun or forget to complete are scheduled less often.

iOS learns when your user opens the app and tends to refresh shortly before. A rarely used app gets few background runs, which is why background tasks are an optimisation, never the only route to fresh data.
BGContinuedProcessingTask lets a task the user started, like an export or a large upload, keep running after they leave the app, with system progress UI and a cancel button.

On iOS, BGAppRefreshTask handles quick catch-up and BGProcessingTask handles heavy work while charging. Each handler reschedules first, does bounded work, handles expiration and always completes. Foreground sync stays the dependable path, because background time follows how often the user opens the app.

A background URLSession hands uploads and downloads to a system daemon. Transfers continue while your app is suspended, and even after the system terminates it. When they finish, iOS relaunches your app in the background to tell you.

Uploads must come **from a file**, not from memory. For multipart uploads, write each part to its own file and create one task per part. Recreate the session with the same identifier at every launch to reconnect to transfers already in flight.

Implement handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession, keep its completion handler, and call it when the session finishes delivering events. Store which task belongs to which file and part in your database, because the callback may arrive in a brand-new process.

If the user force-quits the app from the app switcher, its background transfers are cancelled. Your saved list of finished parts makes the restart cheap: on the next launch, only missing parts are queued again.
pages.ex: Set isDiscretionary for prefetch so iOS can wait for Wi-Fi and power.

pages.p: Big files on iOS go through a background URLSession, one upload task per part file, so the system keeps transferring while we are suspended. We map tasks to parts in SQLite and reconnect the session on every launch. After a user force-quit, only missing parts are queued again.

reels.title: iOS traps that quietly break sync

pages.p: With complete file protection, files cannot be read while the phone is locked, so background sync fails. Use completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication for the sync database and keychain items: protected at rest, readable after the first unlock.

A push with content-available wakes your app for about 30 seconds, but iOS throttles and coalesces these, especially for apps the user rarely opens. Use them to trigger a pull, and keep foreground sync as the dependable path.
Low Power Mode delays discretionary work, and Low Data Mode marks networks as constrained. Respect both, and let users override them for transfers they started themselves.

The sync database uses completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication so background work can open it after the first unlock. Silent pushes only trigger a pull, and we respect Low Power and Low Data Mode except for transfers the user explicitly started.

title: React Native in depth
blurb: What JS can’t do in the background, and the native split.

reels.title: Why JS can’t own background sync

pages.p: When the OS wakes your app for background work, it starts native code. Booting the JavaScript runtime costs time and memory the OS may not grant, and iOS offers no general way to run JS in the background at all.
Moving a large file through JavaScript means holding it in the JS heap, and a few hundred megabytes is enough to crash the app. Files should cross into native code only as a path.

Keep screens, navigation and UI state in JavaScript. Put scheduling, transfers and ideally the sync engine in native modules. Native code writes progress into SQLite and JavaScript observes it, so both share one source of truth.

In React Native, JavaScript owns screens and state, while scheduling, transfers and the sync engine are native. Native code writes progress to SQLite and JavaScript observes it. File bytes never pass through the JS heap; only paths cross into native code.

reels.title: Three levels of React Native sync

pages.p: For an MVP, react-native-background-fetch or expo-background-task runs short JS jobs, a background upload library handles files, and WatermelonDB provides a sync protocol. It ships fast, but tight time budgets and JS start-up cost hold it back.

At scale, write Turbo Modules that expose enqueueSync and enqueueUpload. Android uses WorkManager underneath; iOS uses BGTaskScheduler and background URLSession. JavaScript only enqueues work and watches the database.

Larger teams write the sync engine once, in Kotlin Multiplatform or Rust, and use it from the native Android app, the native iOS app and the React Native app. One protocol implementation and one test suite, with no drift between platforms.
pages.ex: App Center CodePush was retired in March 2025; EAS Update is the usual replacement.

pages.p: We started with background libraries for speed, then moved to Turbo Modules wrapping WorkManager and BGTaskScheduler as usage grew. With native apps alongside, I would put the sync core in Kotlin Multiplatform from day one to avoid drift between platforms.

title: Backend and scale
blurb: A stateless backend, the change log and surviving your own users.

pages.p: Each sync request carries everything the server needs: the device’s cursor and a batch of operations with op_ids. No session lives on any server, so any instance can answer any request, and you add capacity by adding instances.

Every write produces a change-log entry with a sequence number per partition, usually per tenant or user. A pull is a cheap range read on that log, and partitioning keeps each read small as the log grows.

A transactional outbox table on the server, or Debezium reading the Postgres write-ahead log, turns writes into an ordered stream in Kafka. Search indexing, thumbnails, snapshots and push notifications consume it outside the request path.
Because uploads go straight to object storage through presigned URLs, terabytes of media never pass through your API servers. They handle small JSON and stay cheap to run.

The sync API is stateless: every request carries its cursor and op_ids, so any instance serves any device. Writes land in a partitioned change log, CDC streams them to Kafka for indexing and notifications, and file bytes go straight to object storage. Scaling means adding pods.
After an outage, every device holds a backlog and retries at the same moment, so your own clients become the biggest threat to recovery. Sending one push to every user at once causes the same spike.

Full jitter spreads retries randomly across the backoff window. Coalescing triggers means one device runs one sync, not five. A remote-config kill switch lets you pause sync entirely without shipping a release.

Rate-limit per device and per tenant, and return 429 with Retry-After to set the pace. Spread push fan-out over several minutes, and use collapse keys so a device receives one changes-available message, not fifty.

To prevent retry storms, clients use full-jitter backoff and coalesced triggers, the server rate-limits and returns 429 with Retry-After, and push fan-out is staggered with collapse keys. A remote kill switch lets us pause sync without shipping a release.

One million daily users syncing ten times a day is ten million requests, about **115 per second** on average. Peaks run five to ten times higher, so plan for around a thousand per second, plus room for retry storms.
If each user uploads 20 MB a day, that is **20 TB a day** of ingress, all of it straight to object storage. The interesting costs become storage tiers, CDN egress and deduplication by hash.
Fifty changes per user per day at about 1 KB each is **50 GB a day** of change log. With 90 days of tombstone retention, you need partitioning and archiving from the start.
pages.ex: Say the arithmetic out loud. It is what panels remember.

pages.p: A million daily users syncing ten times a day is about 115 requests per second, with peaks near a thousand. At 20 MB of uploads each, that is 20 TB a day, all direct to object storage. A change log near 50 GB a day needs partitioning from the first day.
Under ten thousand users, one Postgres, one sync API, presigned uploads and last-write-wins are enough. Complexity added early only slows you down.
When reads saturate the primary, add read replicas, plus Redis for idempotency keys and rate limits. Replace frequent polling with push hints, and put downloads behind a CDN.
When first sync gets slow and the change log grows large, partition the log by tenant, stream changes through CDC and serve snapshots from a CDN to new devices.

When one tenant or one region can hurt everyone, shard the database and split traffic into regional cells, with data residency where the law requires it. Every stage is justified by a signal you can measure.

I scale in stages triggered by measured signals: replicas and Redis when reads saturate the primary, a partitioned log, CDC and snapshots when first sync slows, and regional cells when one tenant or region can hurt everyone. Nothing is built before its gate.

title: Security, metrics and testing
blurb: Keeping offline data safe and proving sync works.

pages.p: Background jobs must authenticate without the user. Keep short-lived access tokens and a refresh token in Keystore or Keychain, readable after first unlock. If refresh fails, pause sync and ask the user to sign in when they next open the app.
Encrypt the local database for regulated data, wipe it on logout and keep files inside the app sandbox. Presigned URLs should expire within minutes and allow exactly one object and one method.
The server re-checks authorisation on every pull, validates every payload, verifies file hashes on completion and scans uploads. Deletion requests reach every device through tombstones.

Background auth uses short-lived tokens with a refresh token in Keystore or Keychain, readable after first unlock. Regulated data is encrypted at rest and wiped on logout. Presigned URLs expire in minutes, and the server re-checks authorisation and verifies hashes on every request.
A broken sync system rarely crashes. Data simply stops arriving, and users notice days later. You need numbers that move before users complain.

Track **freshness**, the time since each device last synced, at p50 and p95. Track outbox depth, upload completion rate, conflict rate and background-task expirations, split by app version, platform and manufacturer.
Alert when a release moves those numbers, gate staged rollouts on sync success, trace requests from device to database with OpenTelemetry, and keep a remote kill switch for every sync path.

Our sync SLOs are p95 freshness and zero acknowledged writes lost. Dashboards show outbox depth, upload completion, conflict rate and background-task expirations by app version and manufacturer, and staged rollouts are gated on sync success.

reels.title: Testing a system built to be killed

pages.p: Write the sync engine as a function of database state and server responses. Every conflict, error and retry branch can then be tested deterministically, without a device.

On real phones, kill the app mid-upload, toggle airplane mode, switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, reboot, fill the disk, change the clock and revoke the token. Every case should end with no lost data and no duplicates.

pages.h: Test the OS and the scale
pages.p: Force Doze and standby buckets with adb, simulate background launches in Xcode, test on aggressive OEM phones, and seed a million rows on a low-end device to measure first sync and scrolling.

The sync engine is a pure function of database state and server responses, so every branch has deterministic tests. On devices we run kill, airplane-mode, reboot, low-disk and clock-skew drills, force Doze, and seed a million rows on a low-end phone.

title: The principal interview
blurb: How to talk about decisions, trade-offs and failures.

pages.p: Before naming a technology, state the context: data per user, how long users stay offline, whether data is shared, the team’s skills and the deadline. The right answer depends on these, and saying so is itself the signal.

Name at least two real options and the criteria you weighed: reliability, time to market, cost, team fit and how reversible the choice is. Interviewers want to see the comparison, not just the winner.

Say what you chose and what you accepted as its cost, such as a concurrent settings change occasionally being overwritten. Then say which signal would make you revisit it, and that you recorded it as an architecture decision record.

I frame each decision with the context, at least two options, explicit criteria and the cost I accepted, then name the signal that would make me revisit it. Every one is written as an architecture decision record, so the reasoning outlives the meeting.

reels.title: Native, React Native or a shared core?

pages.p: Background sync is native work in every option, so the choice is really about the UI layer and how much logic you want to share. Framed that way, the trade-offs become clear.

Native Kotlin and Swift suit media-heavy, regulated or platform-heavy apps. React Native suits content and form-driven apps built by a strong JavaScript team that needs speed. A Kotlin Multiplatform or Rust core with native UI suits large organisations with complex sync on both platforms.

PowerSync and ElectricSQL give Postgres-to-SQLite sync quickly. Firestore is fast to start but harder at scale. Build your own when sync is core to the product or compliance demands it; for a small product, buy.

Background sync is native in every option, so the real choice is the UI layer. I pick native for media-heavy or regulated apps, React Native for form-driven apps with a strong JavaScript team, and a shared Kotlin Multiplatform core for complex sync on both platforms.
Panels trust a story about something that broke more than a list of things that worked. Choose an incident you were close to: a retry storm, a failed migration or a gap in synced data.
What users saw. What you found. What you changed, in code and in process. What the numbers looked like afterwards. Keep blame out of it and keep yourself in it.

After an outage, every device retried at once and the API hit several times its normal load. We added full-jitter backoff, 429 with Retry-After, staggered push fan-out and a remote kill switch. The next outage recovered without a spike.
pages.ex: No incident of your own? Describe a failure test you ran instead. Never invent one.

pages.p: When we had a retry storm, I said what users saw, how we traced it to synchronised retries, the four changes we made, and that the next outage recovered without a spike. Four beats, numbers at the end, no blame, and my own role clear.

Sync pushes op_ids and pulls by a server cursor.
Files go as checkpointed multipart uploads to S3.
The OS runs it: WorkManager, BGTask, URLSession.
captions: Lead with the constraint.
Then the source of truth.
Then the protocol.
Then the bytes.
Then the platforms.

reels.title: Retry check
reels.q: What makes retrying a push safe?
options: A client op_id the server dedupes
reels.why: The first request may have succeeded before the network dropped. The server returns the original result.

items.p: UI, a big local DB, the outbox
an arrow from the phone that skips the API
walk one edit, kill halfway, resume

reels.title: The follow-up they always ask

left.label: They ask
items: "A user is offline for three weeks. Then what?"

right.label: You answer
items: Deletes are tombstones with a 90-day TTL
App rebuilds from a CDN snapshot, then pulls deltas

captions: This separates seniors from principals.
Name the TTL, the status code and the recovery path.
